title: Graph Theory: Networks, Paths, Trees & Algorithms
description: The mathematics behind programming, computing, finance, business, and economics — one question at a time. Think it through, then choose A, B, or C, and move on at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the degree of a vertex from an explicit edge list.
questions.question: A simple graph has vertex set {A, B, C, D} and edge set {A-B, A-C, A-D, C-D}. What is the degree of vertex D?
questions.hint: Count how many edges in the list have this vertex as one of their endpoints.
questions.explanation: Vertex D appears in the edges A-D, C-D, so it is incident to 2 edge(s). The degree of D is 2.

questions.learningObjective: Derive the degree sequence of a graph from its edge list.
questions.question: Consider the simple graph on vertex set {A, B, C, D} with edges {A-B, A-C, A-D, B-D, C-D}. Which sequence correctly lists the degrees of all vertices, from highest to lowest?
questions.hint: Tally the number of edges touching each vertex individually, then sort the results.
questions.explanation: Computing the degree of every vertex from the edge list and sorting in descending order gives the degree sequence (3, 3, 2, 2).

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph that has vertices but contains no edges at all?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A graph with at least one vertex but zero edges is called an empty, or edgeless, graph.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: The set of all vertices adjacent to a given vertex v?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: The neighborhood of a vertex v is defined as the set of all vertices directly adjacent to v.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph in which each edge has a specific direction, from one vertex toward another?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: When each edge points from one vertex to another, the graph is called a directed graph, or digraph.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A vertex that has degree exactly 1, meaning it is connected to exactly one other vertex?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A vertex of degree exactly 1 is called a pendant (or leaf) vertex.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A vertex that has degree 0, meaning it is not connected to any other vertex?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A vertex of degree 0 is called an isolated vertex because it has no incident edges at all.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: The number of edges in a graph?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: The size of a graph is defined as its number of edges (as opposed to the order, which counts vertices).

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A rooted tree in which every vertex has at most two children?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A rooted tree in which no vertex has more than two children is specifically called a binary tree.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A subgraph formed by choosing a subset of vertices and keeping exactly the edges of the original graph whose two endpoints are both in that subset?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: An induced subgraph is fully determined by its vertex subset: it retains every original edge whose endpoints both lie in that subset.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A subgraph that includes every vertex of the original graph but possibly only some of its edges?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A spanning subgraph keeps all of the original vertices while possibly removing some edges.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph whose vertex and edge sets are both subsets of another graph's vertex and edge sets?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A subgraph is formed by taking a subset of the vertices and a subset of the edges of a larger graph, as long as every edge's endpoints remain included.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph in which every edge has an associated numerical value representing cost or distance?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: Assigning a numeric weight to every edge, such as cost, time, or distance, defines a weighted graph.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph that allows more than one edge between the same pair of vertices, but does not allow loops?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A multigraph permits parallel edges between the same pair of vertices while still forbidding loops.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A tree that has one designated vertex singled out as its top, or root?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A tree with one vertex designated as the root, from which all other vertices descend, is called a rooted tree.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph that allows both parallel edges between vertices and loops at a single vertex?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A pseudograph is the most general case: it allows both multiple edges and loops.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A vertex in a rooted tree that has no children?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A vertex with no children in a rooted tree is called a leaf, matching the pendant-vertex idea in an unrooted tree.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: Among all spanning trees of a weighted connected graph, the one whose total edge weight is smallest?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: The specific spanning tree that minimizes the sum of edge weights is called a minimum spanning tree, distinguishing it from spanning trees in general.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: The smallest number of vertices that must be removed to disconnect a connected graph (or reduce it to a single vertex)?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: Vertex connectivity measures the minimum number of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph, and is a standard measure of robustness.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: The smallest number of edges that must be removed to disconnect a connected graph?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: Edge connectivity measures the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects the graph.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A spanning subgraph of a connected graph that is itself a tree, touching every vertex with the fewest possible edges?
questions.hint: Match the description carefully to the precise definition used in graph theory.
questions.explanation: A spanning tree is a spanning subgraph that is also a tree — connected, acyclic, and touching every vertex using exactly n - 1 edges.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize standard graph-theory definitions and terminology.
questions.question: Which graph-theory term describes the following: A graph on n vertices in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one edge?

questions.learningObjective: Identify the common degree of every vertex in a regular graph.
questions.question: A cycle graph C_9 (a single cycle passing through all 9 vertices) is regular. What is the degree of every vertex in C_9?
questions.hint: Picture the vertices arranged in a ring — each one connects to exactly two neighbors.
questions.explanation: In a cycle graph, every vertex is connected to exactly two neighbors (the vertex before and after it around the cycle), so C_9 is 2-regular.

questions.question: A star graph on 7 vertices has one central vertex connected directly to each of the other 6 vertices, which are connected only to the center. What is the degree of the central vertex?

questions.learningObjective: Determine the edge count of a vertex-induced subgraph.
questions.question: A graph has vertex set {A, B, C, D, E, F} and edges {A-C, A-D, A-F, B-C, B-D, B-E, B-F, C-E, E-F}. Consider the subgraph induced by the vertex subset {C, E, F}. How many edges does this induced subgraph contain?

questions.learningObjective: Compute the maximum number of edges for a simple graph of given order.
questions.question: A graph has order 6 (that is, it has 6 vertices). What is the maximum possible number of edges (size) in a simple graph of this order?
questions.hint: The maximum number of edges equals the number of ways to choose 2 vertices out of the total.
questions.explanation: In a simple graph every pair of the 6 vertices can be joined by at most one edge, giving C(6,2) = 6(5)/2 = 15 as the maximum number of edges.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about completeness using order, size, and the maximum edge bound.
questions.question: A simple graph has 9 vertices and 12 edges. The maximum possible number of edges for a simple graph on 9 vertices is 36. Based on this, is the graph necessarily a complete graph?

options.label: A
options.text: No — completeness depends only on the number of vertices, not the number of edges

options.label: B
options.text: No — it has fewer edges than the maximum, so it cannot be complete

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — any connected graph on this many vertices is automatically complete

questions.hint: Compare the given edge count to n(n-1)/2, the maximum possible for a simple graph of that order.
questions.explanation: A simple graph on 9 vertices is complete only when it has exactly 36 edges (every pair of vertices adjacent). Since this graph has 12 edge(s), it does not have the maximum, so it is not complete.

questions.explanation: For an undirected graph, every edge contributes exactly two 1-entries to the adjacency matrix (position (u,v) and position (v,u)). So the number of edges is 20 / 2 = 10.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret structural graph properties from features of an adjacency matrix.
questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? An adjacency matrix where every row and every column sums to the same value k.
questions.hint: Recall what symmetry, or a nonzero diagonal entry, means for the edges it encodes.
questions.explanation: When every row (and column) sum equals the same value k, every vertex has degree k, which is exactly the definition of a k-regular graph.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret structural graph properties from features of an adjacency matrix.
questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? An incidence matrix of a graph, where rows represent vertices and columns represent edges.

options.label: A
options.text: Each column contains exactly one nonzero entry

options.label: B
options.text: Each row must sum to zero

options.label: C
options.text: Each column contains exactly two nonzero entries, marking the two endpoints of that edge

questions.hint: Recall what symmetry, or a nonzero diagonal entry, means for the edges it encodes.
questions.explanation: In an incidence matrix, each edge column has a nonzero entry in exactly the two rows corresponding to its endpoints, since every edge connects exactly two vertices.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret structural graph properties from features of an adjacency matrix.
questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? An adjacency matrix with a nonzero entry on the main diagonal, at position (L,L).

options.label: B
options.text: There is a loop at vertex L

questions.hint: Recall what symmetry, or a nonzero diagonal entry, means for the edges it encodes.
questions.explanation: A nonzero diagonal entry (L,L) records an edge from vertex L back to itself — a loop.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret structural graph properties from features of an adjacency matrix.
questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? Checking whether two specific vertices F and L are adjacent, using each representation.

options.label: A
options.text: This is an instant O(1) lookup with an adjacency matrix, but may require scanning a neighbor list with an adjacency list

options.label: B
options.text: Adjacency cannot be checked directly from either representation

options.label: C
options.text: This is always faster with an adjacency list than with an adjacency matrix

questions.hint: Recall what symmetry, or a nonzero diagonal entry, means for the edges it encodes.
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix allows checking entry (F,L) directly in constant time, while an adjacency list may require scanning through vertex F's neighbor list to see whether L appears.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret structural graph properties from features of an adjacency matrix.
questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? An entry with a value greater than 1 at position (A,C) in an adjacency matrix.

options.label: A
options.text: There is exactly one edge between vertex A and vertex C

options.label: B
options.text: There are multiple parallel edges between vertex A and vertex C

options.label: C
options.text: Vertices A and C are not adjacent

questions.hint: Recall what symmetry, or a nonzero diagonal entry, means for the edges it encodes.
questions.explanation: A value greater than 1 records more than one edge between the same pair of vertices, which is only possible in a multigraph or pseudograph, not a simple graph.

questions.explanation: When the matrix is not symmetric, an edge can exist from L to G without one existing from G to L, which is the defining feature of a directed graph.

questions.question: In an adjacency matrix representation of a graph, what does the following indicate? An adjacency list representation compared to an adjacency matrix representation for a sparse graph (one with relatively few edges).

options.label: A
options.text: Both representations always use exactly the same amount of memory

options.label: B
options.text: The adjacency list typically uses less memory, since it only stores existing edges

options.label: C

questions.learningObjective: Classify a vertex sequence as a walk, trail, path, or cycle.
questions.question: Consider the sequence of vertices A B D F C E, traced along existing edges of a graph. What is the most specific term that describes this sequence?
questions.hint: Check whether vertices repeat, whether edges repeat, and whether the sequence returns to its start.
questions.explanation: The sequence A B D F C E is a path (every vertex in the sequence is distinct, and therefore every edge used is distinct as well).

questions.learningObjective: Count the connected components of a graph from its edge list.
questions.question: A graph has vertex set {A, B, C, D, E, F, G} and edges {A-D, A-E, A-F, B-G, C-G}. How many connected components does this graph have?
questions.hint: Group vertices together whenever a path of edges connects them, then count the groups.
questions.explanation: Grouping vertices that can reach each other via a sequence of edges yields 2 separate connected component(s): {A, D, E, F}; {B, C, G}.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a bridge by testing whether its removal disconnects the graph.
questions.question: A graph has vertex set {A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H} and edges {A-G, A-H, B-H, C-G, D-E, D-F, D-G, F-H}. If edge B-H is removed, what happens to the graph?

options.label: A
options.text: The graph becomes disconnected, so this edge is a bridge

options.label: B

questions.hint: Remove the edge mentally and check whether every remaining vertex can still reach every other.
questions.explanation: Removing edge B-H splits the graph into more than one connected component, which means B-H is a bridge (an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components).

questions.explanation: A tree is a connected, acyclic graph, and every tree on n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges. Here n = 12, so the tree has 12 - 1 = 11 edges.

questions.learningObjective: Trace the order in which DFS visits vertices from a given start vertex.
questions.question: A graph has neighbor lists (each vertex's neighbors given in alphabetical order): A: [D]; B: [G, H]; C: [D, E]; D: [A, C, F, H]; E: [C]; F: [D]; G: [B]; H: [B, D]. Starting from vertex A, and always visiting available neighbors in alphabetical order, what is the DFS traversal order of the vertices?

options.label: C
options.text: \(A \to D \to C \to E \to F \to H \to B \to G\)

questions.hint: Simulate DFS step by step starting at A, always breaking ties alphabetically.
questions.explanation: Starting at \(A\), DFS recursively visits the alphabetically first unvisited neighbor and backtracks only when necessary. Therefore, the traversal order is \(A \to D \to C \to E \to F \to H \to B \to G\).

questions.learningObjective: Trace the order in which DFS visits vertices from a given start vertex.
questions.question: A graph has neighbor lists (each vertex's neighbors given in alphabetical order): A: [D, E]; B: [C, H]; C: [B, D, G]; D: [A, C]; E: [A]; F: [G]; G: [C, F]; H: [B]. Starting from vertex A, and always visiting available neighbors in alphabetical order, what is the DFS traversal order of the vertices?
questions.hint: Simulate DFS step by step starting at A, always breaking ties alphabetically.
questions.explanation: DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking: from A it moves to the first unvisited alphabetical neighbor, and keeps going deeper until it must backtrack, giving the order A -> D -> C -> B -> H -> G -> F -> E.

questions.learningObjective: Trace the order in which BFS visits vertices from a given start vertex.

questions.question: Evaluate the following statement about Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs: "A graph can be Hamiltonian without being Eulerian, and Eulerian without being Hamiltonian, because the two properties depend on different structural conditions." Which option best reflects the truth of this statement?

options.label: B
options.text: Every Hamiltonian graph must also be Eulerian

options.label: C
options.text: Every Eulerian graph must also be Hamiltonian

questions.hint: Remember that Eulerian properties are about edges, while Hamiltonian properties are about vertices.
questions.explanation: Being Eulerian depends on vertex degrees (all even, or exactly two odd), while being Hamiltonian depends on the existence of a vertex-visiting cycle; neither property implies the other in general.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the edge-based Eulerian property from the vertex-based Hamiltonian property.
questions.question: Evaluate the following statement about Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs: "The Eulerian property of a graph depends only on vertex degrees and connectivity, while the Hamiltonian property has no simple degree-based test in general." Which option best reflects the truth of this statement?

options.label: A
options.text: Both properties can always be checked with the same degree-based test

options.label: C
options.text: Neither property can be tested efficiently for any graph

questions.hint: Remember that Eulerian properties are about edges, while Hamiltonian properties are about vertices.
questions.explanation: Eulerian graphs are characterized exactly by degree parity plus connectivity, but no simple necessary-and-sufficient degree condition is known for Hamiltonian graphs in general, which is what makes Hamiltonicity a much harder problem in practice.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the edge-based Eulerian property from the vertex-based Hamiltonian property.
questions.question: Evaluate the following statement about Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs: "A complete graph K_8 with 8 >= 3 is always Hamiltonian, but is only Eulerian when 8 is odd." Which option best reflects the truth of this statement?

options.label: B
options.text: A complete graph is Eulerian for every value of n

options.label: C
options.text: A complete graph is never Hamiltonian

questions.hint: Remember that Eulerian properties are about edges, while Hamiltonian properties are about vertices.
questions.explanation: In K_8 every vertex has degree 8 - 1. A Hamiltonian cycle always exists in K_8 for 8 >= 3, but an Euler circuit requires every vertex to have even degree, which happens only when 8 - 1 is even, that is, when 8 is odd.

questions.question: Evaluate the following statement about Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs: "A complete bipartite graph K(m,n) is Hamiltonian only when its two parts have equal size, but a wider range of these graphs can still have an Euler circuit." Which option best reflects the truth of this statement?

options.label: A
options.text: K(m,n) is never Eulerian under any circumstances

options.label: B
options.text: K(m,n) is always Hamiltonian regardless of the sizes of its two parts

options.label: C
options.text: This is essentially correct — K(m,n) needs m = n for a Hamiltonian cycle, but is Eulerian whenever both m and n are even

questions.hint: Remember that Eulerian properties are about edges, while Hamiltonian properties are about vertices.
questions.explanation: A Hamiltonian cycle in K(m,n) must alternate between the two parts, which forces them to be equal in size; separately, every vertex's degree in K(m,n) equals the size of the opposite part, so an Euler circuit exists precisely when both m and n are even.

options.label: B
options.text: This is true for both properties, since a disconnected graph cannot have any spanning cycle or a single closed walk covering all edges

questions.hint: Try alternating two colors around the cycle and see whether the last vertex clashes with the first.
questions.explanation: A cycle with an even number of vertices can be properly 2-colored by alternating colors around the cycle. questions.explanation: A cycle with an even number of vertices can be properly 2-colored by alternating colors around the cycle. A cycle with an odd number of vertices cannot: alternating colors forces the last vertex to clash with the first, so a third color is required. Since 16 is even, C_16 has chromatic number 2.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the chromatic number of a small graph by testing proper colorings.
questions.question: A graph has vertex set {A, B, C, D, E} and edges {A-B, A-D, B-D, C-E, D-E}. What is its chromatic number?
questions.hint: Look for the largest clique in the graph as a lower bound, then try to find a matching proper coloring.
questions.explanation: Testing colorings from smallest to largest shows that the vertices cannot all be properly colored with fewer than 3 colors, but a proper coloring using 3 colors does exist, so the chromatic number is 3.

questions.explanation: In a complete bipartite graph K_{2,7}, each of the 2 vertices in the first part connects to all 7 vertices in the second part, giving 2 x 7 = 14 edges in total.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the Handshaking Lemma to a social-network friendship scenario.
questions.question: At a small gathering of 6 people, the number of other attendees each person is friends with (their friendship count) is: A=3, B=4, C=3, D=2, E=2, F=2. Modeling friendships as a graph where people are vertices and mutual friendships are edges, how many total friendship pairs (edges) exist?
questions.hint: Add up everyone's friendship count, then divide by two, since each friendship is counted from both sides.
questions.explanation: This is the Handshaking Lemma applied to a social network: the sum of everyone's friendship counts equals twice the number of friendship pairs. The counts sum to 16, so the number of friendship pairs is 16 / 2 = 8.

questions.learningObjective: Model an exam-scheduling conflict scenario as graph coloring and find the chromatic number.
questions.question: A school must schedule exams for Math, Physics, Chemistry, Biology. Some pairs of exams share students and cannot be scheduled at the same time: Math-Physics, Math-Chemistry, Math-Biology, Physics-Chemistry, Physics-Biology. Modeling exams as vertices and conflicts as edges, what is the minimum number of exam time slots needed so that no conflicting exams overlap?
questions.hint: Treat this as a graph-coloring problem: the minimum number of slots equals the chromatic number of the conflict graph.
questions.explanation: This is a graph-coloring problem: each color represents a time slot, and no two adjacent (conflicting) exams may share a color. The chromatic number of the conflict graph is 3, so the minimum number of time slots needed is 3.
